before.value: Requests may require special appointment handling because of the charge, court, or custody situation, and any legal or policy issue should stay in review until it is resolved. Special case types can require extra fields, such as juvenile, jail-based, or conflict cases, and emergency filings may need a faster path even if the full packet is not complete yet. If information is missing, staff can mark the request as incomplete and either hold it for follow-up or route it to review depending on how critical the missing item is. New staff should be trained to spot incomplete or emergency requests and to handle exceptions without losing the audit trail. The job aid should clearly list situations that stop normal processing, including a conflict, missing required information, an emergency filing, a questionable eligibility issue, or an attorney who is unavailable or over workload limits. It should be paused, rerouted, or escalated when anything breaks normal flow, like missing information, a conflict, an attorney not meeting the qualification for that court or case type, workload limits being reached, or a special case that needs supervisory review. Anything time-sensitive, like a detention matter or a court deadline, should still be handled quickly, but not by skipping the review rules if the assignment would be improper. The main boundary is whether the staff can make the appointment confidently under the standard rules; if not, it needs an exception path with documentation and review. If any of those pieces are missing or if the rotation rules don’t clearly point to an eligible attorney, they should stop and escalate rather than make a guess. That’s especially true when the request crosses into a special appointment category or anything outside the normal pool rules.

before.value: Day-to-day ownership should sit with the county, probably through the Office of Attorney Appointments or whichever IT support group they designate, because they’re the ones running the process every day. The vendor should handle defects, configuration support, and upgrades for anything inside the solution itself, while justice-community partners would mainly own corrections to the data or services they provide. Ownership shifts only when the issue sits outside the county’s control, such as a partner system outage, a data feed problem, or when a vendor fix is needed versus a business process fix. For anything in the gray area, the county should coordinate the handoff so staff always know who is responsible and nothing gets dropped.

before.value: Requests may require special appointment handling because of the charge, court, or custody situation, and any legal or policy issue should stay in review until it is resolved. Special case types can require extra fields, such as juvenile, jail-based, or conflict cases, and emergency filings may need a faster path even if the full packet is not complete yet. If information is missing, staff can mark the request as incomplete and either hold it for follow-up or route it to review depending on how critical the missing item is. New staff should be trained to spot incomplete or emergency requests and to handle exceptions without losing the audit trail. The job aid should clearly list situations that stop normal processing, including a conflict, missing required information, an emergency filing, a questionable eligibility issue, or an attorney who is unavailable or over workload limits. It should be paused, rerouted, or escalated when anything breaks normal flow, like missing information, a conflict, an attorney not meeting the qualification for that court or case type, workload limits being reached, or a special case that needs supervisory review. Anything time-sensitive, like a detention matter or a court deadline, should still be handled quickly, but not by skipping the review rules if the assignment would be improper. The main boundary is whether the staff can make the appointment confidently under the standard rules; if not, it needs an exception path with documentation and review. If any of those pieces are missing or if the rotation rules don’t clearly point to an eligible attorney, they should stop and escalate rather than make a guess. That’s especially true when the request crosses into a special appointment category or anything outside the normal pool rules. The transition also needs to account for emergency and exception paths. If something is missing, inconsistent, or the matter belongs to a different court, office, or appointment path, it should be routed or held until the missing information is resolved. I’d also expect any sealed, juvenile, or special-restriction issue to trigger extra review before anyone moves forward.

before.value: A status trail should show who currently owns the request, who last touched it, and when it moved from one step to the next. If it’s sent back for missing information, it should clearly show that it is awaiting correction and from whom, including whether it is with the court, jail, or our office. If it’s handed off to another staff member or partner, the history should preserve the full chain of custody, not just the current owner, so reviewers can see where it stalled and who was responsible at each point. If a request needs resubmission, the system should keep the original request linked to the corrected version so the history is preserved. The audit trail has to follow the case no matter which workflow it sits in, including moves from old to new workflow or back again, with clear cross-references so old and new histories can be tied together without ambiguity. Audit information should remain searchable during the transition. The system should let staff replace the attorney without losing the original appointment history, so there’s a clear record of who was assigned, when, and why it changed. It should also capture the reason for the change, update the current active appointment, and notify the affected parties so everyone has the same information. If the change is due to a conflict or withdrawal, the old appointment should be closed out cleanly before the new one becomes active, so the audit trail stays intact and there’s no confusion about who represented the defendant at each point.

before.value: Paused, rerouted, or escalated when anything breaks the normal flow, including missing information, a conflict, an attorney not meeting the qualification for that court or case type, workload limits being reached, or a special case needing supervisory review.
